chunks: Why source and body are tied. The question: Which two terminals are often connected together and why?
On almost every discrete MOSFET, the source and the body are shorted together inside the package.
This keeps the junctions around the channel safely blocked and keeps the threshold voltage steady. The price is a built-in diode from source to drain, called the body diode.
Think of a high-jump bar whose height is measured from the floor. If the floor under the jumper could sink, the jump needed to clear the bar would keep changing.
The body is that floor, and the threshold voltage is the bar height. Bolting the floor to the source keeps the bar where the datasheet says.
The catch is that the bolt also creates a one-way flap, the body diode, that lets current slip backward when the voltage is reversed.
A P+ body contact sits right next to the N+ source and one metal strap shorts them. The two red diodes are the body-source and body-drain junctions (anode = P body).
Shorting S to B leaves the body-source diode permanently at 0 volts. The body-drain diode remains and becomes the "body diode" between S and D.
Body (substrate): the silicon the channel is built in. PN junction: the boundary between P-type and N-type silicon (two differently treated kinds).
It acts like a diode, a one-way valve for current. Body effect: the threshold voltage shifts when the source is not at the same voltage as the body.
Body diode: the diode formed between body and drain once the body is tied to the source. V SB : the voltage from source to body.
Tie an NFET's body to its source, so V SB equals 0 . The threshold voltage then stays at its normal value, and the source-body junction can never conduct by accident.
Now pull the drain below the source by more than about 0. 7 volts while the gate is off. The body diode conducts anyway, so one MOSFET can block current in only one direction.
That is why battery protection circuits put two MOSFETs back to back. That is the whole idea.
"Source and body. Discrete MOSFETs short them internally.

It keeps the source-body PN junction from ever forward-biasing, and it removes the body effect: if the source sits above the body, the threshold voltage goes up, so with V SB equals 0 the threshold stays put.
The cost is the body diode from source to drain, so one FET only blocks one direction.
In ICs, NMOS bodies usually share the grounded substrate, so you often can't tie them and have to live with the body effect."
